author: high
claim: The full Vandermonde determinant identity in PROBLEM.md is solved directly by induction using descending column operations.
evidence: Induct on n. For n=1, the determinant of the 1 by 1 matrix (1) is 1, equal to the empty product. Let n>=2 and assume the identity for n-1 real numbers. Starting with the displayed n by n matrix, for k=n,n-1,...,2 replace the kth column by the kth column minus x_1 times the (k-1)st column. Each operation preserves the determinant, and descending order ensures the (k-1)st column still has its original entries x_i^{k-2}. Thus the first row becomes (1,0,...,0), while for i>=2 and k>=2 the new (i,k) entry is x_i^{k-1}-x_1x_i^{k-2}=(x_i-x_1)x_i^{k-2}. Expanding along the first row leaves a lower-right determinant. Factoring x_i-x_1 from its row indexed by i for each i=2,...,n yields the factor product_{j=2}^n(x_j-x_1) times the Vandermonde determinant for x_2,...,x_n. By induction the latter is product_{2<=i<j<=n}(x_j-x_i). Multiplying gives product_{1<=i<j<=n}(x_j-x_i). No division or distinctness hypothesis is used, so repeated values are included.
